subject: AI & Agents
title: AI Can't Do Common Sense
description: A fast breakdown of AI Can't Do Common Sense for builders.

hook.text: Ask AI 'can a crocodile run a steeplechase?' It might analyze the question instead of just laughing.

buildup.text: Common sense requires vast implicit knowledge about physics, society, and everyday experience.

discovery.text: LLMs capture some common sense from text, but physical intuition and social norms often elude them.

twist.text: A child knows a heavy ball will break a glass. AI needs millions of examples to learn what a toddler intuits.

climax.text: The common sense problem is one of AI's oldest unsolved challenges — first identified in the 1960s.

punchline.text: Brilliance without common sense. The smartest fool in the room.

quiz.question: Why is common sense so difficult for AI?
options: It requires vast implicit knowledge about physics and everyday experience
AI already has perfect common sense
Common sense can be learned from text alone

details.summary: AI lacks the common sense that humans acquire through lived experience. It can process information rapidly but fails at basic reasoning that even young children handle effortlessly.
details.whyItMatters: Common sense failures limit AI reliability in unpredictable real-world situations. Understanding this gap prevents over-reliance on AI for tasks requiring situational judgment.
takeaways: AI lacks basic common sense reasoning abilities
Physical world understanding remains a major AI weakness
Common sense is easy for humans but extremely hard for machines

faq.question: Why is common sense so hard for AI?
faq.answer: Common sense involves vast implicit knowledge about how physical and social worlds work. Humans learn this through embodied experience. Encoding it all explicitly for machines has proven extraordinarily difficult.

faq.question: Can large language models use common sense?
faq.answer: LLMs approximate common sense in many language tasks but still fail on basic physical reasoning and unusual scenarios. They match patterns from text rather than genuinely understanding the world.
